title: Printing Variables and f-strings
summary: Combine text and variables in output with commas, +, f-strings, and format specifiers.
intro: Real output mixes words with values: a name, a score, a price. This lesson shows the three ways to build those lines in Python and how to make numbers look exactly right.

steps.title: Commas and +
steps.body:
Most output mixes fixed text with values. The quickest way is commas: `print()` puts one space between its arguments and accepts numbers as they are.

```python
city = "Lima"
year = 2024
print("City:", city, "Year:", year)  # City: Lima Year: 2024
```

The `+` operator joins strings exactly as written, with no space added, so you type the spaces yourself. It only joins text to text, so a number must go through `str()` first.

```python harness
city = "Lima"
year = 2024
{{code}}
```

```python
print("City: " + city + " Year: " + str(year))  # City: Lima Year: 2024
# print("Year: " + 2024)  # TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
```

A common slip is `"City:" + city`, which prints `City:Lima` because `+` never adds a space. Use commas for quick output and `+` when you want exact control over every character.

example.title: Student line
example.prompt: Print a student's name and age with commas, then the same line built with + and str(age).
example.code:
name = "Maya"
age = 19

print("Name:", name, "Age:", age)
print("Name: " + name + " Age: " + str(age))
example.output:
Name: Maya Age: 19
Name: Maya Age: 19
example.explanation: The first `print()` gets four arguments and puts a space between each one, so `"Name:"` and `name` are spaced for you. The second builds one string with `+`, so the spaces live inside the quotes (`"Name: "` and `" Age: "`), and `str(age)` turns `19` into `"19"` so it can be joined.

practice.title: Stock line
practice.prompt:
Print a product's name and stock count two ways.

1. Print the line with commas: `"Product:"`, `product`, `"In stock:"`, `stock`.
2. Print the same line again, built with `+` and `str(stock)`.

Expected output:

```text
Product: Desk lamp In stock: 42
Product: Desk lamp In stock: 42
```
practice.starter:
product = "Desk lamp"
stock = 42

# TODO: print the line with commas
# TODO: print the same line with + and str()
practice.solution:
product = "Desk lamp"
stock = 42

print("Product:", product, "In stock:", stock)
print("Product: " + product + " In stock: " + str(stock))

tests.output:
Product: Desk lamp In stock: 42
Product: Desk lamp In stock: 42

hints: Commas add the spaces for you. With `+`, put the spaces inside the quotes.
`+` only joins text to text, so wrap the number in `str()` before joining it.

steps.title: f-strings
steps.body:
An f-string is a string with an `f` before the opening quote. Each `{name}` inside it is replaced by that variable's value, numbers included, so you need no `str()` and no spacing tricks. This is the form you will use most.

```python
item = "pen"
count = 3
print(f"You bought {count} {item}s")  # You bought 3 pens
```

To print a real brace, double it: `{{` prints `{` and `}}` prints `}`.

```python harness
item = "pen"
count = 3
{{code}}
```

```python
print(f"{{item}} is {item}")  # {item} is pen
```

Put `=` after a name inside the braces to get a debug line with the name and its value. Strings show their quotes, and spaces around `=` are kept.

```python harness
item = "pen"
count = 3
{{code}}
```

```python
print(f"{count=}")    # count=3
print(f"{item=}")     # item='pen'
print(f"{count = }")  # count = 3
```

Forget the `f` and Python prints the braces as plain text: `"{count}"` is just the word in braces.

example.title: Player greeting
example.prompt: Greet a player with one f-string, print a template line with literal braces, and print a debug line for the score.
example.code:
name = "Ana"
level = 3
score = 98

print(f"Hello {name}, you are level {level}!")
print(f"Template: {{name}} = {name}")
print(f"{score=}")
example.output:
Hello Ana, you are level 3!
Template: {name} = Ana
score=98
example.explanation: `{name}` and `{level}` are swapped for their values. In the second line `{{name}}` is an escaped brace pair, so it prints `{name}` as text, while the plain `{name}` after it is replaced. `{score=}` prints the variable name, an equals sign, and the value.

practice.title: Order confirmation
practice.prompt:
Print an order confirmation with f-strings.

1. Print `Order for Ben: 4 x notebook` using `customer`, `quantity`, and `item` in one f-string.
2. Print the literal text `{qty}` next to the real quantity: `Placeholder {qty} = 4`.
3. Print a debug line for `quantity` with `=` inside the braces.

Expected output:

```text
Order for Ben: 4 x notebook
Placeholder {qty} = 4
quantity=4
```
practice.starter:
customer = "Ben"
item = "notebook"
quantity = 4

# TODO: print the three lines with f-strings
practice.solution:
customer = "Ben"
item = "notebook"
quantity = 4

print(f"Order for {customer}: {quantity} x {item}")
print(f"Placeholder {{qty}} = {quantity}")
print(f"{quantity=}")

tests.output:
Order for Ben: 4 x notebook
Placeholder {qty} = 4
quantity=4

hints: Start each string with `f` so the braces are filled in.
Double each brace that should print as plain text.
For the debug line, put `=` right after the name inside the braces, with no spaces.

steps.title: Format specifiers
steps.body:
Add a colon and a format spec inside the braces to control how a value looks: `{value:spec}`.

| Spec | What it does | Code | Prints |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `.2f` | fixed 2 decimal places | `{3.14159:.2f}` | `3.14` |
| `,` | thousands separator | `{1500000:,}` | `1,500,000` |
| `04` | zero pad to width 4 | `{7:04}` | `0007` |
| `.1%` | times 100, 1 decimal, % sign | `{0.256:.1%}` | `25.6%` |

A number in the spec sets a minimum width. Put `<`, `>`, or `^` in front of it to align left, right, or center (an odd leftover space goes on the right). Without one, text lines up on the left and numbers on the right.

```python
name = "Ana"
print(f"[{name:<6}]")  # [Ana   ]
print(f"[{name:>6}]")  # [   Ana]
print(f"[{name:^6}]")  # [ Ana  ]
```

Width and precision combine: `{price:>8.2f}` right-aligns a 2 decimal number in 8 columns, which lines prices up in a column. Longer values are never cut. They just overflow.

Two gotchas. `.2f` rounds the stored binary value, so `f"{2.675:.2f}"` prints `2.67`. And the checker ignores spaces at the end of a line, so padding after the last value never shows: pad columns that have something after them.

example.title: Price list
example.prompt: Print a centered title, two aligned price rows with zero-padded IDs, a population with commas, and a discount as a percent.
example.code:
title = "Price List"
id_1, name_1, price_1 = 7, "Pen", 1.5
id_2, name_2, price_2 = 42, "Backpack", 34.99
population = 8336817
discount = 0.15

print(f"{title:^30}")
print(f"{id_1:04} {name_1:<10} {price_1:>8.2f}")
print(f"{id_2:04} {name_2:<10} {price_2:>8.2f}")
print(f"Population: {population:,}")
print(f"Discount: {discount:.1%}")
example.output:
Price List
0007 Pen            1.50
0042 Backpack      34.99
Population: 8,336,817
Discount: 15.0%
example.explanation: `{title:^30}` centers 10 characters in 30 columns, so 10 spaces go on each side (the trailing ones are invisible). `{id_1:04}` turns `7` into `0007`. `{name_1:<10}` pads the name to 10 columns, and `{price_1:>8.2f}` shows 2 decimals right-aligned in 8 columns, so both prices line up. `:,` groups digits by thousands and `:.1%` turns `0.15` into `15.0%`.

practice.title: Scoreboard
practice.prompt:
Print a formatted scoreboard with format specifiers.

1. Print `header` centered in 24 columns.
2. Print one row per player, Mia first, then Leo: the name left-aligned in 8 columns, one space, the score zero-padded to 4 digits, one space, then the time right-aligned in 6 columns with 2 decimal places.
3. Print `Total:`, a space, and `total` with thousands separators.
4. Print `Average:`, a space, and `average` with 2 decimal places.
5. Print `Accuracy:`, a space, and `accuracy` as a percent with 1 decimal place.

Expected output:

```text
       Scoreboard
Mia      0950   9.50
Leo      0087  12.25
Total: 1,234,567
Average: 7.46
Accuracy: 87.5%
```
practice.starter:
header = "Scoreboard"
name_1, score_1, time_1 = "Mia", 950, 9.5
name_2, score_2, time_2 = "Leo", 87, 12.25
total = 1234567
average = 7.456
accuracy = 0.875

# TODO: print the six lines with format specifiers
practice.solution:
header = "Scoreboard"
name_1, score_1, time_1 = "Mia", 950, 9.5
name_2, score_2, time_2 = "Leo", 87, 12.25
total = 1234567
average = 7.456
accuracy = 0.875

print(f"{header:^24}")
print(f"{name_1:<8} {score_1:04} {time_1:>6.2f}")
print(f"{name_2:<8} {score_2:04} {time_2:>6.2f}")
print(f"Total: {total:,}")
print(f"Average: {average:.2f}")
print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.1%}")

tests.output:
Scoreboard
Mia      0950   9.50
Leo      0087  12.25
Total: 1,234,567
Average: 7.46
Accuracy: 87.5%

hints: Each line is one f-string with a spec after a colon, as in the price list.
In a row, the name needs `<` with a width, the score needs `0` with a width, and the time needs `>`, a width, and `.2f`, as the prices do.
The last three lines use `,`, `.2f`, and `.1%` after the colon.

recap:
- `print("Label:", value)` puts a space between arguments.
- `+` joins strings with no space, and numbers need `str()` first.
- `f"Hi {name}"` fills in values, `{{` and `}}` print braces, `{x=}` prints a debug line.
- `{x:.2f}` fixed decimals, `{n:,}` thousands, `{n:04}` zero padding, `{p:.1%}` percent.
- `{s:<10}`, `{s:>10}`, `{s:^10}` align in a width, and `{price:>8.2f}` combines width and precision.
